report:
**Conclusion: yes—with an important qualification.** Systemic “cortisone-like” drugs (corticosteroids), especially low-dose dexamethasone, increase survival for *hospitalized patients with severe or critical COVID-19 who need oxygen or mechanical ventilation*. They are not a general treatment for mild COVID-19.

The pivotal randomized RECOVERY trial compared dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days with usual care. In patients already on invasive mechanical ventilation, 28-day mortality was 29.3% with dexamethasone versus 41.4% with usual care (rate ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.51–0.81)—an absolute reduction of about 12 deaths per 100 treated. Mortality was also lower in those receiving oxygen without invasive ventilation. There was *no benefit* in patients not needing respiratory support. This is strong causal evidence because treatment was randomized.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436

A WHO-coordinated meta-analysis of randomized trials in critically ill patients similarly found that systemic corticosteroids reduced 28-day all-cause mortality versus usual care/placebo, supporting that the finding was not dependent on one trial or one particular steroid.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32876694/

Accordingly, WHO makes a strong recommendation for systemic corticosteroids in severe and critical COVID-19, but suggests against them in non-severe disease. Steroids suppress harmful inflammation in advanced COVID-19, but can also impair immune responses and cause adverse effects (for example, high blood glucose and secondary infections), so timing and clinical severity matter.  
https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/module-3-corticosteroid-therapy-and-covid19.pdf
